heading: Which compiler each language uses
body:
A service in Rust, Go, C#, F#, Swift, Kotlin, Java, Dart or Ruby reaches the browser as WebAssembly. A release build (`ty build` or `ty bundle`) compiles each of these languages with the compiler and settings that make the smallest download. `ty preview` keeps fast settings, so a change shows up in about a second. After a release build, `ty build` prints one line for each language: which compiler it used and why (ADR 0081; an ADR is an architecture decision record).

| Language | Release build | Why this compiler | Development build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rust | rustc with `opt-level=z`, LTO and one codegen unit, then Binaryen `wasm-opt -Oz` | rustc already makes small modules; these settings and `wasm-opt` remove what is left | rustc with `opt-level=s` |
| Swift | swiftc with `-Osize` and the static standard library, then Binaryen `wasm-opt -Oz` | swiftc makes a module without Foundation; `wasm-opt` removes what is left | swiftc with `-Osize`, no Binaryen |
| Go | TinyGo with `-opt=z`, then `wasm-opt -Oz` | TinyGo leaves out most of the Go runtime, so the module is many times smaller | the standard Go compiler |
| C# and F# | the trimmed .NET interpreter, with Emscripten `-Oz` | the interpreter is the smallest .NET download and fast enough for state and logic | no native relink |
| Kotlin | the Kotlin/Wasm production build, with Binaryen | Kotlin's own production step makes the program about three times smaller | no Binaryen |
| Java | javac, TeaVM's WasmGC backend, then Binaryen `wasm-opt -Oz` | TeaVM keeps only the Java classes the service uses; `wasm-opt` makes the module about half as large | TeaVM, no Binaryen |
| Dart | `dart compile wasm -O4` | `-O4` also drops runtime type checks, so the module is smaller and faster | `-O2`, with the type checks |
| Ruby | the pinned mruby runtime | one runtime for every Ruby service, built once on your machine | the same |

Binaryen (its `wasm-opt` program) and TinyGo are optional. Without them a release build still works; the module is larger, and the build line says what to install. `ty doctor` lists both when your project has a Rust, Go, Swift or Java web service.
